name: Harrison's Rocks
text: Your train passes near Harrison's Rocks, on the train's {side}, a line of sandstone crags in the woods south of Groombridge. Climbers own them, through the British Mountaineering Council since 2009, and the soft rock has about 400 short climbs, all done on a top rope.

name: Jarvis Brook
text: Your train passes near Jarvis Brook, on the train's {side}, the village where Crowborough station actually stands; the village grew when the station opened. Its brickworks closed in 1980, and the quarry that fed them became a local nature reserve in 2009.

name: Iron furnace near Buxted
text: Your train passes near the remains of an iron furnace, on the train's {side}, a scheduled monument from the days when the Weald made England's iron. Buxted was at the heart of it: the first cast-iron cannon made in England was cast near the village in 1543, by Ralf Hogge.

name: Buxted
text: Your train passes near Buxted, on the train's {side}. In the early 1800s the Prime Minister Lord Liverpool bought Buxted Park and enlarged it, pressing the villagers to leave their houses: by 1836 the old village centre had gone, and only its church stayed in the park.

name: Littlehampton
text: Your train passes near Littlehampton, on the train's {side}, a fishing town at the mouth of the Arun that became a port and resort, with a ferry across the Channel to Honfleur. Its population grew tenfold in the 1800s, from 584 in 1801 to 5,954 in 1901.

name: Littlehampton Lifeboat Station
text: Your train passes near Littlehampton Lifeboat Station, on the train's {side}, on the east bank of the Arun. The RNLI opened a station here in 1884; its inshore lifeboat of 1967 was paid for by an appeal on BBC TV's Blue Peter and named Blue Peter I.

name: London Bus Museum
text: Your train passes near the London Bus Museum at Brooklands, on the train's {side}. About 35 of its buses and coaches are on show, from Victorian horse-drawn omnibuses to Routemasters, including the only surviving wartime utility bus that ran in London.

name: White Mill, Sandwich
text: Your train passes near White Mill, on the train's {side}, a smock mill west of Sandwich built in 1760. It last worked by wind in 1926 and by an oil engine until 1957, and is now a rural heritage centre, with the miller's cottage furnished as it was between 1900 and 1939.

name: Harefield Road
text: Your train passes the site of Harefield Road, a station planned in the late 1930s for the Central line's extension to Denham. The war stopped the work, and afterwards the green belt ruled out the new houses it was meant to serve, so it was never built.

name: RAF West Ruislip
text: Your train passes the site of RAF West Ruislip, on the train's {side}, a depot chosen in 1917 for the Royal Flying Corps and split in two by this line. The US Air Force took it over in 1955 and the US Navy in 1975; after the Navy left in 2006 it was cleared for housing.

name: RAF South Ruislip
text: Your train passes the site of RAF South Ruislip, on the train's {side}, the headquarters of the US Air Force's Third Air Force from 1949 to 1972. In 1970 three teenagers whose fathers were stationed here, Dewey Bunnell, Dan Peek and Gerry Beckley, formed the band America.

name: Orley Farm School
text: Your train passes near Orley Farm School, on the train's {side}, founded in 1850 to prepare boys for Harrow School. In 1862 it took its name from Anthony Trollope's novel Orley Farm, which describes the buildings and grounds the Trollope family once owned and the school later used.

name: Sudbury Town Underground station
text: Your train passes near Sudbury Town Underground station, on the train's {side}, rebuilt by Charles Holden in brick, concrete and glass in the early 1930s. It first opened in 1903, on the first of the Underground's surface lines to run electric trains instead of steam.

name: Wembley Stadium
text: Your train passes near Wembley Stadium, on the train's {side}, England's national football stadium, opened in 2007 where the old Wembley stood from 1923 to 2000. With 90,000 seats it is the largest stadium in the UK, and its arch carries more than three quarters of the roof's weight.

name: Lord's Cricket Ground
text: Your train passes near Lord's Cricket Ground, on the train's {side}, the third ground Thomas Lord opened, in 1814: his second had to go when the Regent's Canal was cut through its outfield. The pitch has a pronounced slope, running down from north to south.

name: Abbey Road Studios
text: Your train passes near Abbey Road Studios, on the train's {side}, opened by the Gramophone Company in November 1931 behind a Georgian townhouse. The Beatles were its most famous clients, working mostly in Studio Two, and the building was listed in 2010 when it was under threat of sale.

name: The More
text: Your train passes near the site of The More, on the train's {side}, a palace owned by Cardinal Wolsey and then Henry VIII, where Catherine of Aragon lived in the winter of 1531 to 1532. In 1527 the French ambassador thought it more splendid than Hampton Court; nothing now remains above ground.

name: Heathrow Terminal 5
text: Your train passes near Heathrow Terminal 5, on the train's {side}, opened in 2008 after the longest public inquiry in British history. Its main building, designed by the Richard Rogers Partnership, is the largest free-standing structure in the UK.

name: Heathrow Terminal 4
text: Your train passes near Heathrow Terminal 4, on the train's {side}, built for £200 million south of the southern runway and opened by the Prince and Princess of Wales on April 1st 1986. British Airways was based here until 2009, when it moved to the airport's newest terminal.

name: Heathrow Terminal 1
text: Your train passes near Heathrow Terminal 1, on the train's {side}, designed by Frederick Gibberd and opened by Queen Elizabeth II in April 1969, when it was the largest new airport terminal in western Europe. It closed in 2015 to make way for a bigger Terminal 2.

name: Bedfont Lakes Country Park
text: Your train passes near Bedfont Lakes Country Park, on the train's {side}, 72.5 hectares of lakes, meadows and woodland. Gravel was dug here from the 1860s and it was a landfill site until 1973; it became a nature reserve in 2000, and is home to 156 species of bird.

name: Feltham marshalling yard
text: Your train passes the site of Feltham marshalling yard, on the train's {side}, a hump yard built with the help of about 200 German prisoners of war and opened in 1918 to sort freight for south-west London. It closed in 1969, and part of the site is being rebuilt to stable South Western Railway's trains.

name: Hounslow Heath
text: Your train passes near Hounslow Heath, on the train's {side}, all that remains of a heath that once spread across Feltham, Hounslow, Twickenham and what is now Heathrow. Armies camped on it, Cromwell's in 1647 among them, and in the 17th and 18th centuries it was notorious for highwaymen.

name: Worton Hall (Isleworth Studios)
text: Your train passes near Worton Hall, on the train's {side}, a house of 1783 that became a film studio in 1914. Alexander Korda made Things to Come here in 1936, from H. G. Wells's screenplay; the studios closed in 1952.

name: Whitton Park
text: Your train passes near the site of Whitton Park, on the train's {side}, the estate of the 3rd Duke of Argyll, whom Horace Walpole nicknamed the Treemonger. After his death in 1761 many of his trees went to the Princess of Wales's new garden at Kew; a black locust planted there in 1762 still survives.

name: All Hallows, Twickenham
text: Your train passes near All Hallows church, on the train's {side}, which has the tower of Wren's All Hallows Lombard Street. When that City church was demolished in 1937, its tower, bells, cloister and many fittings were moved here, and a new church was built around them.

name: Strawberry Hill House
text: Your train passes near Strawberry Hill House, on the train's {side}, the Gothic villa Horace Walpole built up in stages from 1749 to suit his collection of antiquities. Its style, Strawberry Hill Gothic, foreshadowed the Victorian Gothic Revival.

name: Fulwell bus garage
text: Your train passes near Fulwell bus garage, on the train's {side}, built in 1902 and 1903 as a tram depot for London United Tramways. London's first trolleybuses arrived here in 1931, and it later became London Transport's main trolleybus works.

name: Bushy Park
text: Your train passes near Bushy Park, on the train's {side}, the second largest of London's Royal Parks, which Henry VIII made a deer-hunting ground. In the Second World War General Eisenhower planned the D-Day landings from his headquarters in the park, and herds of red and fallow deer still live here.

name: Sandycombe Lodge
text: Your train passes near Sandycombe Lodge, on the train's {side}, the country retreat J. M. W. Turner designed and built in 1813 and lived in from 1814 to 1826. It is the only surviving building he designed.

name: Richmond Railway Bridge
text: Your train crosses the Thames on Richmond Railway Bridge, one of the first railway bridges over the river, opened in 1848 to Joseph Locke's design. Doubts about its cast iron led to a rebuilding in steel from 1906 to 1908, keeping much of the original look.

name: Palm House, Kew Gardens
text: Your train passes near the Palm House at Kew Gardens, on the train's {side}, finished in 1848 and the first greenhouse built on such a scale. It was also the first large-scale use of wrought iron in a building, and many of its tropical plants are endangered or extinct in the wild.

name: Crawdaddy Club
text: Your train passes near the Station Hotel, on the train's {side}, whose back room became the Crawdaddy Club in 1963. The Rolling Stones were its house band in its first year, followed by the Yardbirds; the club took its name from Bo Diddley's song Doing the Craw-Daddy.

name: Mortlake Brewery
text: Your train passes near Mortlake Brewery, on the train's {side}, where brewing is recorded as early as 1487. As it grew in the 1850s it supplied India Pale Ale to the British army in India, and it brewed Budweiser from 1995 to 2011, before closing in 2015.

name: Mausoleum of Sir Richard and Lady Burton
text: Your train passes near the tomb of the explorer Sir Richard Burton, on the train's {side}, a mausoleum of marble and stone shaped like a tent, designed by his wife Isabel. Their coffins can be seen through a glass panel at the back.

name: The Bull's Head, Barnes
text: Your train passes near the Bull's Head, on the train's {side}, a riverside pub in Barnes, rebuilt in 1846, that opened as a jazz venue in 1959. It became one of the most important jazz venues in Britain, known as the suburban Ronnie Scott's.

name: Barnes Railway Bridge
text: Your train crosses the Thames on Barnes Railway Bridge, first opened in 1849 to Joseph Locke's design; it also carries a footpath. It is a landmark of the Boat Race, and its coat of arms has a light blue oar for Cambridge and a dark blue oar for Oxford.

name: Q Theatre
text: Your train passes the site of the Q Theatre, on the train's {side}, by Kew Bridge, which put on new plays from 1924 to 1958. Vivien Leigh, Dirk Bogarde and Joan Collins began their stage careers here, and it staged Terence Rattigan's first plays.

name: London Museum of Water & Steam
text: Your train passes near the London Museum of Water & Steam, on the train's {side}, in Kew Bridge Pumping Station, opened in 1838 to supply west London with drinking water. It has the world's largest collection of Cornish engines, including the largest surviving single-cylinder beam engine in the world.

name: Firestone Tyre Factory
text: Your train passes the site of the Firestone Tyre Factory, on the train's {side}, an Art Deco landmark on the Great West Road opened in 1928. It was demolished over the August bank holiday in 1980, reportedly before it could be listed, which led to the listing of 150 interwar buildings; its gates and railings survive.
